newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.S. to veto Jerusalem resolution for second time.
newsitem.headline: U.S. to veto Jerusalem resolution for second time.

text.p: For the second time in two weeks, the United States will veto a Security Council resolution late on Friday calling on Israel to halt construction of Jewish housing in Arab East Jerusalem, U.S. ambassador Bill Richardson said.
"The Security Council will be voting later today on an Arab-sponsored resolution. The United States will be voting no," he told reporters.

"This is consistent with the American view that the Security Council is not a proper forum for debate on these issues. The parties themselves are those that should deal with these very, very important issues," Richardson added.
On March 7 the United States vetoed a resolution calling on Israel to abandon plans to build 6,500 homes for Jews on land captured during the 1967 Middle East war.
The site, between Jerusalem and Bethlehem, is called Jabal Abu Ghneim in Arabic and Har Homa in Hebrew.
All 14 other council members voted for the resolution, sponsored by the council's four European Union members -- Britain, France, Portugal and Sweden.

The United States, chief sponsor of Middle East peace negotiations, has criticised Israel's action as undermining trust between the parties. But it has also argued that differences between Israel and the Palestinians should be resolved between them and not brought to the United Nations or other international bodies.

After the March 7 U.S. veto, Arab states took the issue to the General Assembly, where there is no veto. On March 13 the Assembly adopted a resolution by a vote of 130 to 2 with 2 abstentions, calling on Israel not to go ahead with the project. The United States and Israel cast the only negative votes.
When Israeli surveyors and bulldozers began work on the site on Tuesday the 22-member Arab group brought the issue back to the Security Council and drafted a new, briefer resolution.

It would demand that Israel "immediately cease construction of the Jabal Abu Ghneim settlement in East Jerusalem, as well as all other Israeli settlement activities in the occupied territories." Secretary-General Kofi Annan would be asked to report on developments.

During two days of private consultation on the Arab group's request for a meeting, council members considered whether, instead of voting on the resolution and ending up with an almost certain U.S. veto, it might be possible to reach agreement on a statement to be read by the council president calling on Israel not to proceed with its building.
A statement, which required the concurrence of all 15 council members, does not carry the same weight as a formal resolution.
Arab states, represented in the council by Egypt, strongly favoured pressing the resolution to a vote.
The United States, opposed to any resolution, was prepared to go along with a council statement if suitable wording could be agreed.

When council president Zbigniew Wlosowicz of Poland announced an evening meeting on Friday to vote on the draft, he also said members "expressed their revulsion at the terrorist bombing" which took place in Tel Aviv earlier in day when a suicide bomber blew up a cafe, killing three people and wounding more than 40. He said council members expressed their condolences to the families of the victims.
